title: Binary Search & Variations
oneLiner: Logarithmic search strategy dividing sorted search space in half with boundary convergence.
imagePrompt: Minimal diagram of sorted array with left, mid, right pointers halving search space

body.definition: Binary Search finds a target within a sorted collection by repeatedly comparing the target to the middle element and eliminating half the remaining search space in O(log n) time.
body.whyItMatters: Reduces search time from O(n) linear scans to O(log n). Critical for monotonic search spaces, range queries, rotated sorted arrays, and optimization problems using binary search on answer.
body.commonPitfall: Using (l + r) / 2 causes integer overflow in languages with bounded integer types. Always calculate mid with l + (r - l) / 2.
body.interviewAngle: Tested via rotated sorted array search, lower/upper bound insertion points, and optimization over monotonic predicates.

quickChecks.question: What mathematical property must the search space satisfy for binary search to work?
quickChecks.answer: Monotonicity (elements or predicate results must be ordered/sorted).

quickChecks.question: Why use l + (r - l)/2 instead of (l + r)/2?
quickChecks.answer: To prevent integer overflow when l + r exceeds max integer capacity.

title: Two Pointers Technique
oneLiner: Linear traversal pattern using dual indices converging or moving in tandem to eliminate nested loops.
imagePrompt: Array diagram with left and right indices meeting at center

body.definition: The Two Pointers pattern coordinates two memory indices that traverse a sequential data structure from opposite ends, same direction (fast/slow), or across two separate arrays.
body.whyItMatters: Converts O(n^2) brute-force nested iterations into optimal O(n) single passes with O(1) auxiliary memory by leveraging sorted properties or cycle geometry.
body.commonPitfall: Applying opposing two pointers on unsorted arrays without sorting first, leading to invalid pointer decisions.
body.interviewAngle: Essential for 2Sum/3Sum problems, container with most water, palindrome checks, and in-place array compaction.

quickChecks.question: What is the space complexity of two pointers on an in-place array problem?
When can opposite-end pointers NOT be applied?
quickChecks.answer: When the array is unsorted and element order is arbitrary.

title: Sliding Window Pattern
oneLiner: Dynamic subarray boundary optimization maintaining state across contiguous subranges in linear time.
imagePrompt: Sliding window frame expanding and contracting across array

body.definition: Sliding Window maintains a contiguous subarray or substring bounded by two pointers (left and right) that expands to absorb elements and contracts when constraints are violated.
body.whyItMatters: Avoids recomputing overlapping subsegment statistics from scratch, turning O(n * k) or O(n^2) algorithms into O(n) linear scans with running frequency hash maps.
body.commonPitfall: Failing to update state (e.g. character frequencies or running sum) during window contraction, causing desynchronized metrics.
body.interviewAngle: Frequently tested in longest substring without repeating characters, minimum window substring, and max sum subarrays.

quickChecks.question: Why is the time complexity of sliding window O(n) despite nested loops?
quickChecks.answer: Because each pointer (left and right) visits each element at most once.

quickChecks.question: What distinguishes fixed-size window from dynamic window?
quickChecks.answer: Fixed maintains constant length k; dynamic expands/contracts based on a condition.

title: Monotonic Stack Pattern
oneLiner: LIFO stack preserving strictly ascending or descending order to compute nearest greater or lesser elements.
imagePrompt: Stack diagram maintaining monotonically decreasing bar heights

body.definition: A Monotonic Stack maintains elements in monotonic order (strictly increasing or decreasing) by popping elements that violate the order before inserting the new element.
body.whyItMatters: Computes next greater/smaller element for every item in an array in O(n) total time with O(n) space, eliminating quadratic O(n^2) nested scans.
body.commonPitfall: Storing values instead of element indices in the stack, making it impossible to resolve distances or update the result array accurately.
body.interviewAngle: Appears in Daily Temperatures, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, and Trapping Rain Water.

quickChecks.question: What stack order is used to find Next Greater Element?
quickChecks.answer: Monotonically decreasing stack (top of stack holds smallest element seen so far).

quickChecks.question: What is the amortized cost per element in a monotonic stack?
quickChecks.answer: O(1) amortized because each element is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Trie (Prefix Tree)
oneLiner: Tree-based data structure storing re-traversable string prefixes for fast prefix matching and autocomplete.
imagePrompt: Multi-way prefix tree with character edges and word termination flags

body.definition: A Trie is a multi-way search tree where each node represents a character along string paths, sharing common prefixes among multiple keys.
body.whyItMatters: Provides O(L) time complexity for insert, search, and prefix matching (where L is key length), independent of the number of words N in the dataset.
body.commonPitfall: Allocating fixed 26-element arrays per node when character sets are sparse or Unicode, causing immense memory overhead.
body.interviewAngle: Foundational for search autocomplete, spell checkers, IP routing longest prefix match, and Boggle word searches.

quickChecks.question: What is the lookup time complexity of a word of length L in a Trie?
quickChecks.answer: O(L) operations, strictly bounded by word length.

quickChecks.question: Why is a Trie preferred over a Hash Set for autocomplete?
quickChecks.answer: Trie can query all keys starting with a prefix in O(prefix + results) time.

title: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
oneLiner: Linear ordering of DAG vertices respecting directional dependency constraints using in-degree reduction.
imagePrompt: Directed acyclic graph resolving dependencies via in-degree queue

body.definition: Topological Sort orders vertices of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u appears before vertex v in the sequence.
body.whyItMatters: Resolves compilation orders, build pipelines, database migration ordering, and task scheduling with prerequisite constraints in O(V + E) time.
body.commonPitfall: Failing to check if the result length equals V. If fewer vertices are emitted, a directed cycle exists in the graph.
body.interviewAngle: Classic Course Schedule I & II problems, package dependency resolution, and spreadsheet formula evaluation order.

quickChecks.question: Can a graph with directed cycles have a topological sort?
quickChecks.answer: No. Topological sort exists if and only if the graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

quickChecks.question: How does Kahn's algorithm detect cycles?
quickChecks.answer: If the processed vertex count is less than total vertices V, a cycle exists.

title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
oneLiner: Near constant-time data structure tracking partitioned elements into disjoint subsets with path compression.
imagePrompt: Disjoint set trees flattening depth via path compression

body.definition: Union-Find (DSU) maintains a collection of disjoint sets supporting two primary operations: find (identify representative set root) and union (merge two distinct sets).
body.whyItMatters: Achieves nearly O(1) amortized time complexity O(α(n)) using path compression and union by rank/size. Essential for Kruskal's MST and dynamic connectivity.
body.commonPitfall: Omitting path compression or union by rank, which degrades performance to O(n) per operation resembling a skewed linked list.
body.interviewAngle: Standard approach for number of connected components, redundant connection detection, and Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree.

quickChecks.question: What is the amortized time complexity of DSU with path compression and rank?
quickChecks.answer: O(α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function (effectively constant < 5).

quickChecks.question: How does DSU detect an undirected cycle when adding edge (u, v)?
quickChecks.answer: If find(u) === find(v) prior to union, adding the edge creates a cycle.
